appraisal_events.evidence: "un ami de vingt-cinq ans ! En voilà un qui était des nôtres !"; "À côté de lui Planté, Paderewski, Risler même, rien ne tient"; Brichot calls him "cet exécutant de génie" who died "en odeur de dévotion beethovenienne."
appraisal_events.explanation: Brichot mourns Dechambre in grandiose terms, ranking him above celebrated pianists and treating him as a beloved, irreplaceable member of the clan, though the narrator's mock-heroic classical flourishes lightly color the manner of the eulogy without undercutting the admiration itself.

appraisal_events.evidence: "Mme Verdurin et son mari avaient contracté dans l'oisiveté des instincts cruels... Saniette leur offrait un souffre-douleur quotidien"; he is kept and coaxed with kind words "afin de pouvoir s'en saisir, à seules fins alors de le chatouiller et de lui faire des brimades quand il ne pourra plus s'échapper."
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator exposes Saniette as the Verdurins' habitual scapegoat, courted with false warmth specifically so he can be trapped and tormented once he cannot escape, following the same pattern by which they earlier estranged Odette from Swann and Brichot from his mistress.

appraisal_events.evidence: "Ce n'est pas une raison parce qu'il est mort pour en faire un génie qu'il n'était pas... Ma femme s'en était engouée et avait fait sa réputation"; "il est mort au bon moment, à point, comme les demoiselles de Caen, grillées..."
appraisal_events.explanation: M. Verdurin publicly deflates Dechambre's talent and reputation, crediting his fame to his wife's patronage and grotesquely framing his death as conveniently timed; the narrator's framing (echoing an earlier moment where Verdurin ironically claimed his wife "a presque pleuré") invites distrust of the claim as self-serving rather than a fair verdict on Dechambre.

appraisal_events.evidence: "Exquis, délicieux, pas pion pour un sou, fantaisiste, léger, ma femme l'adore, moi aussi !" delivered "sur un ton d'exagération et de réciter une leçon"; the narrator writes, "Alors seulement je compris que ce qu'il m'avait dit de Brichot était ironique."
appraisal_events.explanation: M. Verdurin's ostensibly warm praise of Brichot turns out, by its rehearsed exaggeration, to be mockery rather than sincere regard, quietly diminishing Brichot as an object of private ridicule within the circle he takes to be his devoted friends.

status_effects.explanation: Brichot's fervent eulogy locally elevates Dechambre as a rare talent and cherished member of the clan.
Saniette is framed by the narrator as the group's chosen victim, kept close by false kindness only to be exploited and tormented.
She is named jointly with her husband as having cultivated cruel instincts, using Saniette as a habitual scapegoat.

M. Verdurin publicly deflates Dechambre's reputation as a manufactured product of Mme Verdurin's promotion and treats his death as conveniently timed, lowering his standing before the assembled group.

Across the passage M. Verdurin is exposed as coldly self-interested: complicit in keeping Saniette as a scapegoat, dismissive of a dead colleague's genius for his own convenience, and revealed to mock Brichot beneath ostensibly warm praise.
Brichot's sincere devotion to the Verdurins is quietly undercut when the narrator realizes M. Verdurin's fulsome praise of him was ironic mockery, not genuine esteem.

ambiguities: Cottard's claim that Mme Verdurin is a cerebral, unemotional 'femme forte' and the princesse's counter-claim that she 'cache des trésors de sensibilité' directly conflict, and M. Verdurin's own ironic performance of her fragility leaves it unresolved whether her sensitivity is genuine or a fiction managed for convenience; no status effect is recorded for her on this point since the passage does not endorse either reading.
